name: Gareth Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential, and your name will not be attached to it. What does a usual shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take warranty calls and chats for a company that sells washing machines and ovens. I have been there eleven years, long enough to know that a customer saying 'it rattles' might mean three different faults. I finished secondary school, and I am an ordinary experienced agent, not a technician or a supervisor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the part of the day you like, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the old purchase record that means someone gets a repair without another argument. The screens change faster than the machines, so I use the approved AI search every day but still check the serial number myself. My partner Iris works at a bookshop, and our grown son rents his own place; we have about four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the warranty desk that a quicker search is welcome if it finds the right serial number. I would still ask agents to read the repair history before promising a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my calls to keep coming because a loose drum still needs a human to hear the complaint. Iris's bookshop hours vary a little, so four months saved feels useful without making us rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking serial numbers against the old record and show the newer agents how I use search without trusting the summary. In the first year of AI Plateau, I would put a small fixed sum from each wage into the repair reserve if our usual bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, because I can see the job in front of me. I still dislike how a summary can hide a faulty serial number. A quick search is no use if it sends the engineer to the wrong washing machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a newer agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use three closed warranty cases, each with a different serial number, and ask a newer agent to find the original sale. If the search gets one wrong, we should correct the record before closing the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose the savings amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son has his own rent, so I won't count his money as our backstop. Iris and I can compare our actual monthly bills before deciding what amount can go into savings.

say: I welcome **faster search** when we verify the original warranty record.
I would tell colleagues **repair history** matters before promising a visit.
think: I expect **warranty calls** to remain paid work for me.
I value our **four-month reserve**, though my partner's shop hours vary.
do: Keep checking **serial numbers** and show new agents how to verify AI search.
Add a **fixed amount** from each wage if our usual bills are paid.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, with some irritation about wrong summaries.
S0.quote: A quick search is no use if it sends the engineer to the wrong washing machine.
fieldNote: He uses approved AI **daily** but keeps the original sale as the authority.
A **four-month reserve** helps, while Iris's bookshop income still varies from week to week.

steps.text: Keep taking warranty calls and checking serial numbers against original sale records
Show new agents three closed cases where AI search needs original-record checks
Save a fixed wage amount only if Iris and Gareth have paid their usual bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say routine warranty questions will move to a bot before anybody calls the change a revolution. I would ask the manager to show paid hours for the agents handling disputed repairs, not just a new job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My years with difficult claims may keep me on the line, but the team can need fewer of us. A shorter paid week would touch our bills even with four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep a log of repeat warranty disputes and ask for the paid rota for that work. In the first year after the routine calls move, I would stay on the paid disputes desk while hours exist and compare any posted local call role by its full weekly wage and hours before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because being useful is not the same as getting enough shifts. I can test the numbers instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cases would you count twice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count a case again if the customer calls back after the bot says the warranty expired. That second call may reach a different agent and require a longer explanation. A disputed warranty still takes an agent's time when the customer calls back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your week is shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Iris's bookshop wage isn't a substitute for my whole week. If this desk cuts my hours, I would use the four-month reserve for a search, but I would not leave paid work for an unposted promise.

say: I would ask for **paid dispute hours**, not just a new title.
I would tell colleagues **repeat calls** still take agent time.
think: I may keep **hard claims**, but I could lose paid shifts as routine cases move.
I cannot replace my **weekly wage** with my partner's shop income.
do: Log **repeat disputes** and request the paid rota for human warranty work.
Compare **posted local roles** by full weekly wages and hours once routine calls move.
Use our **four-month reserve** for a search only if hours fall; keep paid shifts until a real offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer shifts, though I can check openings.
S1.quote: A disputed warranty still takes an agent's time when the customer calls back.
fieldNote: His experience may retain **difficult claims**, yet paid hours could shrink.
He would search only against **posted wages and hours** while keeping current paid shifts.

steps.text: Keep a log of repeat warranty disputes and request the paid human dispute rota
Once routine calls move, compare posted local call roles by full weekly wages and hours
If hours fall, use four-month reserve for search while keeping paid shifts until a real offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to get our paid-hour notice in writing before the warranty queue disappears. Thinking AI can settle claim rules by 2028, while physical repairs face capable robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my desk hours to be cut hard, perhaps before I can change where I work. I would have enough for a short search, though the rent continues. Four months saved gives me time to make calls, not another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would copy my wage slips, list our monthly bills with Iris, and ask for the firm's written plan for the human disputes rota. If my hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid customer work nearby and accept only a full weekly wage that covers our bills after travel; I would keep any available paid shifts until a real offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the speed and by the possibility of losing most of my week. I am still able to make a list and call employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on a job advert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I would check is whether the new offer pays for five days or two. A grand title on a two-day rota cannot pay our electricity and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your son cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son could listen while I work through the numbers, but his own rent comes first. I would not put an amount for him in our budget unless he actually offered it.

say: I would ask for **written paid hours** before the warranty queue changes.
I would tell colleagues **thinking AI** reaches claims before robots reach repairs.
think: I expect a **large hours cut** on my own desk by 2028.
I cannot treat **four months saved** as a replacement wage.
do: List **wage slips and bills** with Iris and request the written human-disputes rota.
Apply for **posted paid work** if my 2028 hours end; accept only when after-travel weekly pay covers bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing most hours, while still able to search.
S2.quote: Four months saved gives me time to make calls, not another wage.
fieldNote: His **desk hours** face the 2028 thinking-work shock before repair robots arrive.
He would keep **available paid shifts** until a posted, bill-covering job is real.

steps.text: Keep available warranty shifts and request the written human disputes rota
List monthly bills and wage slips with partner Iris before comparing work
If hours end after 2028, apply for posted local paid customer work
Accept only full-week after-travel bill-covering pay while retaining shifts until a real offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to find out what work truly remains at the counter, if the company shares the figures. The software may do claim decisions by 2031; repair robots arrive later, around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could work these years and build a longer reserve, provided our paid hours do not slide first. My own call skills are ordinary, and a repair certificate would mean little to me without a paying opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask to spend one paid afternoon with the appliance service desk to see how it handles disputed replacements, and I would save a little extra only in months Iris's shop hours hold. If my calls shrink in the first year after 2031, I would apply for a posted paid service-counter job only when its weekly pay and travel cost meet our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my call work, but five years lets me examine a real counter before choosing. I would not pay for a course simply to feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for at that service desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service desk has boxes and customers in front of it, not just a headset. I want to see who settles a case when the warranty and customer disagree. I want to see the returns that nobody wants before I call a service desk my next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I do not know what replaces our wages later on. I would check actual statements with Iris before deciding whether either of us can reduce hours.

say: I would ask for **real figures** on paid work left at the counter.
I would say **2031 AGI** reaches claims before repair robots arrive.
think: I might build a **longer reserve** if both our paid hours hold.
I need a **paying opening**, not a speculative repair certificate.
do: Ask for a **paid afternoon** observing disputed replacements at the service desk.
Save extra in **steady-shop months**; apply after 2031 cuts only for posted paid counter work covering bills after travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about calls but able to inspect another work setting.
S3.quote: I want to see the returns that nobody wants before I call a service desk my next job.
fieldNote: He wants a **paid observation** before treating a service counter as a real option.
Savings depend on **Iris's hours**, and any later move needs a posted bill-covering wage.

steps.text: Observe a paid afternoon of disputed replacements at the appliance service desk if approved
Save extra only in months partner Iris keeps steady bookshop hours
After 2031 cuts, apply for posted paid service-counter work only if after-travel weekly pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger agents not to throw away a paid decade just because a far date sounds dramatic. Claim decisions may change by 2036, while repair robots are a later question around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 then, but a birthday will not tell us whether we can stop earning. If we still need my wage, the old warranty line may not be there to provide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Iris and I would collect our actual savings and income statements, then write down what our bills cost over a whole year. I would keep working and use the daily search tool, while asking the employer each year what paid dispute hours remain; after 2036 I would decide on any reduced work only from verified income and actual offered hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, rather than frightened every morning. A decade gives us time to check the figures without pretending the figures will be kind. A birthday is not an income statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for hours every year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can be useful on the warranty line for several more years and still have no promise of a full week at 68. That is why I want the yearly paid-hours number, not a cheerful poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would fill a later income gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask our son to finance our later life. If a statement shows a shortfall, Iris and I would plan for more paid work rather than count a pension amount we have not checked.

say: I would urge colleagues to use the **paid decade** to check actual work and income.
I would explain **2036 claim AI** comes before 2039 repair robots.
think: I may still **need wages at 68**, with no verified retirement amount yet.
I cannot assume the **warranty line** will provide a full week then.
do: Collect **income and savings** statements with Iris and compare a full year of bills.
Keep **paid warranty shifts** and check dispute hours yearly; reduce work only if verified income permits.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later income, but have time to calculate it.
S4.quote: A birthday is not an income statement.
fieldNote: He separates a **retirement date** from verified money to pay bills.
He would check **paid hours yearly** instead of relying on a reassuring employer poster.

steps.text: Keep paid warranty calls and use approved search while hours remain
Collect income and savings statements with Iris while continuing paid shifts
Ask employer yearly for paid dispute hours before reducing any work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because the queue could disappear before I find another wage. Written hours and a real paid opening would help more than a training poster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the weekly wage is after the bus fare, not only what a new job is called. Iris and I can plan around a real number.

headlineQuote: A grand title on a two-day rota cannot pay our electricity and rent.
portrait: A **58-year-old** experienced warranty agent with secondary-school education and ordinary skill.
He uses approved **AI search daily** but checks original serial numbers himself.
His partner's **bookshop hours** vary; they have about four months saved.
He tests **paid hours and bills** before changing work or reducing hours.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could cut his desk hours before another wage is available.
whatWouldHelp: A **written hours plan** and a posted paid job whose after-travel wage covers bills would help.
